title: Sub-20 nm spin textures with arbitrary topological charge stabilized by higher-order interactions
authors: Zhen Sun, Shiwei Zhu, Moritz A. Goerzen, Megha Arya, Changsheng Song, Dongzhe Li
abstract: Topological magnetization textures play a central role in modern magnetism. For many applications, spin textures with different topological charges $Q$ in the same system are particularly attractive. Although the coexistence of skyrmions and antiskyrmions ($|Q| = 1$) has been reported in inversion-symmetric magnets, extending this to high-$Q$ ($|Q| > 1$) textures with arbitrary charge remains elusive. Here, using an atomistic spin model parameterized from first-principles calculations, we predict the emergence of sub-20 nm high-$Q$ textures in Janus monolayers, van der Waals magnets of growing interest. We explore skyrmion and antiskyrmion rings as well as skyrmion bags with $|Q|$ up to 5, and characterize their nucleation mechanisms, thermal stability, and collapse pathways. We find that higher-order spin interactions (HOI), which extend the conventional bilinear-exchange Hamiltonian, are essential for stabilizing these high-$Q$ spin textures. The rings remain thermally stable at zero magnetic field. HOI substantially enhance their energy barriers while leaving their size nearly unchanged and stabilize them even in the absence of Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction. Skyrmion bags, in contrast, nucleate only in the presence of HOI. In particular, the four-spin three-site interaction is the key ingredient preventing high-$Q$ textures from collapsing into the ferromagnetic state. Finally, we identify previously unreported parity-dependent collapse mechanisms for high-$Q$ textures. Our results establish HOI as an overlooked mechanism for high-$Q$ nucleation.
summary: This work predicts that higher-order spin interactions (HOI) are crucial for stabilizing high-topological-charge spin textures (up to $|Q|=5$) in 2D van der Waals magnets at nanoscale dimensions. Using DFT-derived spin models and advanced simulation techniques, the authors demonstrate that these HOI enhance the thermal stability and prevent the collapse of these complex magnetic structures.
main_problem: The primary goal is to extend the stabilization of topological magnetization textures from low topological charges ($|Q|=1$) to high charges ($|Q|>1$) in magnetic materials.
main_result: Higher-order spin interactions (HOI) are shown to be essential for stabilizing these high-$Q$ spin textures, allowing them to exist at sub-20 nm scales and even in the absence of Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction.
method: The study uses atomistic spin models parameterized by first-principles DFT calculations, employing spin simulations (SPINAKER) and Minimum Energy Path (GNEB) calculations to determine stability barriers.
model_or_system: The research focuses on Janus monolayers, specifically van der Waals magnets like MnPCl, modeled by a spin Hamiltonian that includes Heisenberg exchange, DMI, anisotropy, and crucial higher-order terms (biquadratic and four-spin interactions).
key_observables: Topological charge ($Q$), thermal stability, energy barriers ($\Delta E$), and the size/radius of the stabilized spin textures.
important_parameters: Sub-20 nm size scale, the presence/absence of DMI, and the magnitude of the higher-order interaction parameters ($Y_1$).
main_assumptions: Dipole-dipole interactions are neglected, and the model relies on nearest-neighbor interactions for the HOI terms.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate schematic representations of high-$Q$ textures (rings, bags) and show field-dependent phase stability diagrams, comparing energy barriers with and without HOI.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the problem of high-$Q$ stabilization, details the atomistic spin model derived from DFT, presents simulations showing HOI's necessity for stability, and concludes by identifying new collapse mechanisms.
why_interesting: While focused on magnetism, the study of topological stability, energy barriers, and phase transitions in structured quantum materials is relevant to understanding complex many-body dynamics in condensed matter systems.
